title: Severe Pannus Formation with Coronary Artery Obstruction after the Ozaki Procedure: A Case Report.
authors: Yuichiro Kitada; Daniel O'Connor; Koji Takeda
abstract: We report a case of severe pannus formation causing coronary artery obstruction after aortic valve neocuspidization (the Ozaki procedure). A 64-year-old woman who had undergone the Ozaki procedure for aortic stenosis presented with chest pain. She was diagnosed with obstruction of the right coronary artery ostium and moderate aortic regurgitation and stenosis. Redo aortic valve replacement and coronary artery bypass grafting were subsequently performed. Surgery revealed severe circumferential pannus on the aortic side of the neocusps, with obstruction of the right coronary artery ostium. The pannus and cusps were removed completely; after aortic annular enlargement, the aortic valve was replaced. The patient's postoperative course was uneventful. This is the first case report of coronary obstruction due to pannus formation after the Ozaki procedure.

title: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation in the Presence of Aortic Coarctation: Current Evidence and Practical Approaches.
authors: Vilhelmas Bajoras; Artiomas Širvys; Gintarė Petraitytė; Ričardas Kundelis; Liudas Usoris; Giedrius Davidavičius; Sigitas Čėsna
journal: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions
abstract:
Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become an established treatment for severe aortic stenosis across a wide spectrum of surgical risk. As TAVI is increasingly used in younger patients and in those with congenital valve disease, the coexistence of aortic stenosis and untreated coarctation of the aorta (CoA) is being encountered more frequently. However, evidence guiding the procedural strategy in this complex anatomical setting remains limited.
To systematically review the published literature on TAVI in adult patients with untreated or residual coarctation of the aorta, focusing on patient characteristics, procedural strategies, vascular access selection, management of coexisting CoA, and clinical outcomes.
A systematic literature search was performed in PubMed, Wiley Online Library, ScienceDirect, and the Cochrane Library to identify published reports describing TAVI in adult patients with angiographically confirmed native or residual severe CoA. Case reports and case series published between January 2013 and September 2025 were included. Studies involving repaired CoA without restenosis or surgical aortic valve replacement were excluded. Clinical characteristics, access routes, procedural strategies, and outcomes were analyzed.
Nine patients from published reports met the inclusion criteria. Hemodynamically significant CoA was present in five patients (55.6%). Bicuspid aortic valve anatomy was reported in six cases. Transcatheter access routes included transcarotid (44.4%), transfemoral (33.3%), transsubclavian (11.1%), and transaxillary (11.1%) approaches. A staged strategy with initial CoA stenting followed by TAVI was performed in two patients (22.2%), whereas seven patients (77.8%) underwent single-procedure management, including concomitant treatment of both lesions in two cases. Procedural success was achieved in all cases, although technical challenges related to valve delivery and stent expansion were occasionally encountered.
TAVI in patients with untreated or residual CoA is feasible and can be performed with high procedural success when individualized strategies are applied. Access selection and the timing of CoA intervention should be guided by anatomical characteristics and hemodynamic severity. Given the limited evidence base, careful preprocedural planning and a multidisciplinary approach are essential to optimize outcomes in this complex patient population.

title: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Patient Selection, Referral Timing, and Advanced Therapy Options.
authors: Mohammed Abusafia; Shada Jadam; Susan Ospina; Milind Y Desai
abstract: In this review, we provide a detailed up-to-date summary of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). From the complex and diverse presentations to the individualized clinical profiles, we delve into the different aspects of HCM diagnosis, management, and follow up. We discuss imaging modalities and their indications as well as current guidelines for both pharmacological and surgical treatment options. We also review the data regarding emerging therapies.

title: Strategy for Exercise Restriction in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
authors: Hyun-Jung Lee
abstract: This article outlines the evolving evidence and guidelines surrounding exercise in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), challenging the traditional paradigm of universal restriction. It highlights that most patients with HCM can safely engage in physical activity (PA) and improve cardiovascular outcomes. Recent evidence demonstrates that vigorous PA improves functional capacity and does not increase adverse events in most low-risk HCM patients. Contemporary guidelines advocate for individualized exercise recommendations based on comprehensive risk stratification and shared decision-making. A clinical framework is proposed to support tailored exercise prescriptions and shared decision-making.

title: Multimodality Imaging in the Evaluation of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
authors: Jamey Cutts; Christopher Kramer
abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is characterized by pathologic hypertrophy in the absence of a potentially causative disease process and carries increased risk of heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and sudden cardiac death. Synergistic use of multi-modal imaging is pivotal and necessary in the diagnosis and management of patients with, or at risk for, HCM. Echocardiography, cardiac MR, and cardiac computed tomography each have important roles and limitations in assessing the morphologic changes responsible for symptoms and morbidity in HCM. In this article, we will explore these modalities and their roles in evaluating HCM.

title: The Role of Medical Therapy in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: An Updated Review.
authors: Jung-Won Lee; Kyeong-Hyeon Chun; Eui-Young Choi; Jiwon Seo
abstract: This review highlights recent advances in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) treatment, focusing on how to effectively implement both traditional and novel pharmacologic strategies in clinical practice. Traditional medications like beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers continue to play a critical role. However, new treatments, such as cardiac myosin inhibitors, provide an innovative approach for relieving symptoms, especially in obstructive HCM cases. Emerging therapies, including sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, sacubitril/valsartan, and ninerafaxstat, show promising benefits. Proper management of related conditions such as atrial fibrillation and heart failure is also essential. A comprehensive approach that considers individual patient characteristics and the specific subtype of HCM is essential for achieving optimal outcomes.

title: The Evolving Landscape of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Phenocopies and Diagnostic Pathways in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
authors: Jang-Won Son; Jong-Ho Nam; Kang-Un Choi; Geu-Ru Hong
abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is an inherited myocardial disease defined by unexplained thickening and hypertrophy of ventricular myocardium. However, several other conditions-"phenocopies" or mimics-can present with a similar hypertrophic phenotype. This article details the major HCM phenocopies, including infiltrative and storage diseases (amyloidosis, Fabry, Pompe, and Danon), systemic granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis), mitochondrial disorders, physiologic hypertrophy (athlete's heart), and hypertensive heart disease and aortic stenosis. We describe their distinguishing clinical features, multimodality imaging findings, pathophysiology, and key diagnostic clues highlighting red-flag signs and recent advances in diagnostics.

title: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy in the Absence of "Hypertrophy": A Precision Medicine Reappraisal.
authors: Julian Vega-Adauy; Jesús Urbina
abstract: Fixed wall thickness cutoffs have historically defined hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), yet this rigid approach overlooks patients with early, segmental, or morphologically subtle disease. Subthreshold phenotypes-particularly in women, individuals with short stature, and those with apical or focal variants-may not meet conventional criteria despite exhibiting pathologic features. This article examines the limitations of absolute diagnostic thresholds and advocates for a precision medicine framework. Integrating cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with individualized metrics and architectural markers enhances diagnostic accuracy, identifies nonclassical presentations, and facilitates earlier disease recognition, ultimately improving care across the heterogeneous spectrum of HCM.

title: Redefining Left Ventricular Systolic Dysfunction in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Ejection Fraction and Global Longitudinal Strain.
authors: Soongu Kwak; Hyung-Kwan Kim
abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is an inherited disease characterized by increased myocardial thickness without cardiac, systemic, or metabolic causes to explain the observed left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy. Importantly, LV systolic dysfunction influences symptoms, heart failure, and the risk of SCD in HCM. LV global longitudinal strain (LV-GLS) is a sensitive marker for detecting subclinical LV dysfunction and improving risk stratification. Integrating LV-GLS with other imaging biomarkers, such as late gadolinium enhancement and left atrial reservoir strain, may improve risk prediction. Future research should focus on refining LV-GLS cutoffs and exploring its utility for personalized risk assessment in HCM.

title: Risk Factors for Progression in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
authors: Shantanu Sengupta; Aniket Wazade
abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is one of the important causes of sudden cardiac death (SCD) in younger people and athletes. It is important to identify the risk factors for SCD in individuals with HCM. This article, based on recent systematic literature studies, will focus on the risk factors for progression in patients with HCM. The article discusses the established risk factors, such as a family history, unexplained syncope, and some new risk factors. The findings of this article demonstrate that there is a need for further research on individual risk factors and risk stratification in HCM patients remains a clinical challenge.

title: Phenotyping the Many Faces of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
authors: Paul Geenty; Belinda Gray; Liza Thomas
abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the most common inherited cardiomyopathy and is defined by the presence of left ventricular hypertrophy 15 mm or greater in the absence of any other identifiable cause. Beyond this definition, clinical phenotype is heterogeneous, and associated clinical manifestations occur in varying proportions of patients, including left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve with associated mitral regurgitation, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. Accurate clinical phenotyping allows the identification of groups with distinct natural history and prognosis, with risk stratification being crucial for prevention of sudden cardiac death.

title: Transapical Beating-Heart Septal Myectomy for Symptomatic Nonobstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Initial Clinical Experience.
authors: Jing Fang; Yue Chen; Wei Zhou; Rui Li; Chaoyu Gong; Jitai Du; Hui Wang; Qunhui Wang; Lin Cheng; Chen Wang; Taiqiang Chen; Yilei Ma; Ying Zhu; Jianyuan Zhou; Xiaohua Zhu; Hartzell V Schaff; Yani Liu; Song Wan; Xiang Wei
abstract:
Nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (nHCM), defined as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy without left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, remains challenging to treat because of its heterogeneous pathophysiology. This study evaluated the safety and efficacy of transapical beating-heart septal myectomy in patients with symptomatic nHCM.
Patients with symptomatic, drug-refractory nHCM were prospectively enrolled to undergo transapical beating-heart septal myectomy through a left minithoracotomy. Under real-time transesophageal echocardiographic guidance, septal myectomy was tailored to relieve systolic cavity obliteration and mid-to-apical ventricular obstruction and to enlarge the left ventricular cavity. The primary end point was procedural success at 6 to 12 months postoperatively, defined as fulfillment of all prespecified criteria compared with baseline: ≥1-class improvement in New York Heart Association functional class, ≥10-point increase in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score, ≥10-mL increase in stroke volume, and normal or grade I diastolic function.
Between January 2023 and January 2025, 97 consecutive eligible patients with nHCM underwent transapical beating-heart septal myectomy at Tongji Hospital. At postoperative 6 to 12 months, procedural success was achieved in 87.6%. Specifically, New York Heart Association functional class I increased from 0% at baseline to 93.8% at follow-up, the median Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score improved from 64 (interquartile range, 56-69) to 87 (interquartile range, 82-92; P<0.001), the stroke volume increased from 53.5 mL (interquartile range, 41.0-66.6 mL) to 70.8 mL (interquartile range, 61.3-82.3 mL; P<0.001), and normal or grade I diastolic function increased from 65.6% to 97.9%. Among patients who underwent paired cardiopulmonary exercise testing (n=58), peak oxygen uptake increased by 1.1±2.9 mL/kg/min (P=0.008). In an exploratory, hypothesis-generating analysis of 12 patients with paired 13N-ammonia positron emission tomography, coronary flow reserve increased from 1.8±0.3 to 2.0±0.4 (P=0.034). Adverse events included mitral valve injury (n=1) and ventricular septal perforation (n=1), the latter resulting in 1 postoperative death.
Transapical beating-heart septal myectomy was associated with favorable left ventricular geometric remodeling and meaningful improvements in symptoms, health status, and functional capacity in selected patients with symptomatic nHCM. Being a potential therapeutic option for a previously difficult-to-treat population, it warrants further evaluation in controlled, multicenter studies.

title: Transapical Beating-Heart Septal Myectomy for Obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
authors: Xiang Wei; Jing Fang; Song Wan
abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a prevalent heterogenous genetic cardiac disorder. In the cardiac myosin inhibitor era, the guideline-directed management of HCM remains an emerging frontier worldwide. Septal myectomy has been the gold standard treatment option for obstructive HCM over the past 60 years. However, the complexity of this procedure and required expertise (and lack of qualified training) have limited its success and availability beyond high-volume HCM centers. Transapical beating-heart septal myectomy (TA-BSM), a newly developed innovative technique, simplifies conventional septal myectomy by eliminating the need for sternotomy, cardiopulmonary bypass, and aortotomy. Most important, the inclusion of real-time intraoperative echocardiographic guidance and evaluation makes TA-BSM safer, more precise, cost-effective, and reproducible. The apparent advantages of TA-BSM, including substantial reductions in surgical trauma and operating times and much faster postoperative recovery in patients with obstructive HCM, are encouraging. TA-BSM is particularly feasible in patients with long-segment obstruction, or small aortic valve annulus, or in those who had undergone previous cardiac operations. The frequent resolution of systolic anterior motion and associated mitral regurgitation after TA-BSM, without concomitant mitral valve intervention, highlights the central role of intraoperative echocardiography and close surgeon-echocardiographer collaboration in achieving optimal procedural outcomes. Further multicenter evaluation of TA-BSM will help define its role among septal reduction strategies for patients with obstructive HCM.

title: Transcatheter Versus Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement in Dialysis-Dependent Patients With Severe Aortic Stenosis: A GRADE-Assessed Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authors: Adil Nawaz; Muhammad Abbas; Maria Qadri; Munazza Sikandar; Zayna Rehman; Muhammad Usman; Mansoor Khalid; Wasim Khan; Hassaan Abid; Syed Asadullah; Muhammad Qasim; Umama Alam
abstract: The optimal treatment strategy for severe aortic stenosis (AS) in dialysis-dependent patients remains uncertain. We conducted an updated systematic review and meta-analysis comparing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with surgical aortic valve replacement, with certainty assessed using GRADE. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane were searched from inception through June 2026 for comparative studies in dialysis-dependent adults with severe AS. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality, while secondary outcomes included stroke, myocardial infarction, major bleeding, major vascular complications, permanent pacemaker implantation, and intensive care unit and hospital length of stay. Random-effects models were used, with prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses. Eight observational studies involving 13,312 patients were included. TAVR was associated with lower 30-day mortality than surgical aortic valve replacement (risk ratio [RR], 0.64; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.42-0.98; I2 = 88%), although this association was confined to adjusted studies. TAVR was also associated with shorter intensive care unit stay (mean differences, -3.63 days; 95% CI, -5.10 to -2.15) and hospital stay (mean differences, -5.37 days; 95% CI, -8.83 to -2.23), but higher risks of permanent pacemaker implantation (RR, 2.03; 95% CI, 1.42-2.91) and major vascular complications (RR, 2.96; 95% CI, 1.50-5.86). No significant differences were observed in stroke, myocardial infarction, or major bleeding. The certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate. TAVR may offer advantages in early mortality and recovery but carries increased procedural risks, and treatment should be individualized through multidisciplinary Heart Valve Team assessment.

title: Successful percutaneous intervention for post-operative coronary artery stenosis in a child: a case report.
authors: Jacob Gilchrist; Cara Morgan; Abdul Salam; Nathalie Dedieu; Elliot J Smith
abstract:
Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for coronary artery stenosis in young children is rare, and evidence guiding management remains limited. Established indications for PCI in children include reversing or preventing ischaemia, as well as preventing sudden cardiac death. Guidance on optimal revascularization approaches and long-term outcomes remains underreported. We report successful PCI for significant post-operative right coronary artery (RCA) stenosis in a 7-year-old.
The patient presented with acute onset cardiac failure aged 5 years. Echocardiography demonstrated aneurysmal aortic root dilatation with severe aortic regurgitation and left ventricular dysfunction. The aetiology was found to be infectious, and the patient underwent aortic root replacement. The postoperative course was complicated by myocardial ischaemia and right ventricular dysfunction, necessitating RCA re-implantation before discharge. At age 7, although asymptomatic, follow-up imaging demonstrated progressive proximal RCA stenosis. Stress cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed inducible perfusion defects, and exercise testing confirmed dynamic ECG changes consistent with ischaemia. Selective coronary angiography demonstrated critical proximal RCA stenosis. In collaboration with adult interventional cardiologists, PCI with coronary stent implantation was performed successfully, restoring coronary perfusion and improving functional capacity.
This case highlights the feasibility of PCI with coronary stenting for complex post-operative coronary stenosis in paediatric patients. Input from adult interventional cardiologists allowed for technical challenges to be navigated and resulted in restoration of coronary perfusion with substantial improvements to patient quality of life.
