title: Late-Presenting Myocardial Infarction With Separate Anomalous Right-Sided Origins of the Left Anterior Descending and Circumflex Arteries: A Case Report.
authors: Wassim Beladel; Youssef Zeryouh; Mohamed El Minaoui
abstract: The clinical significance of an anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery depends on the proximal course and ostial morphology, not on the ectopic origin alone, and coexisting acute myocardial infarction and multivessel atherosclerotic disease can make culprit assignment and revascularization difficult. A 79-year-old man was diagnosed with a late-presenting high-lateral ST elevation myocardial infarction while being treated for urinary sepsis. He had no ongoing chest pain. The electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with a premature atrial contraction (PAC), a negative T wave in aVL, and a flattened T wave in lead I, and cardiac troponin was 4850 ng/L. Transthoracic echocardiography showed regional wall-motion abnormalities and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45% to 50%. Coronary angiography on day 3 demonstrated a left anterior descending artery arising from the right coronary ostial region with a severe proximal stenosis and a left circumflex artery arising separately from the right coronary sinus with a severe proximal stenosis. The right coronary artery had no significant stenosis. After clinical stabilization and heart team review, elective percutaneous coronary intervention of the proximal left circumflex artery was performed 34 days after diagnostic angiography. A 3.5 x 28 mm everolimus-eluting stent was implanted, and the procedural report documented no significant residual stenosis and final Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction grade 3 flow. Intervention on the anomalous left anterior descending artery was deferred pending coronary computed tomography angiography. This case separates the management of a severe atherosclerotic lesion from risk assessment of an anomalous coronary origin. Invasive angiography did not establish the proximal course of the left anterior descending artery, and an interarterial or intramural course cannot be inferred from its right-sided origin. Because no acute thrombus, pre-intervention flow grade, or definitive culprit lesion was documented, the circumflex artery should be described as the presumed infarct-related artery and the delayed procedure as staged revascularization. Further management of the left anterior descending artery requires cross-sectional anatomical imaging and individualized assessment of ischemia, viability, functional status, and procedural risk.

title: Planned percutaneous coronary intervention around transcatheter aortic valve implantation: a GRADE-assessed meta-analysis of randomized trials.
authors: Ibrahim Gowaily; Abdelrahman Awad; Ahmed A Ibrahim; Mohamed S Elgendy; Ali Bin Abdul Jabbar; Abdalhakim Shubietah; Muhammad Ghallab; Ahmed Elmogy; Mohamed Abuelazm; Ahmed Aboeata
abstract:
Severe aortic stenosis and coronary artery disease frequently coexist in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). We compared planned percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) around TAVI with an initially conservative or deferred PCI strategy.
We searched PubMed, Cochrane, Scopus, and Web of Science through 15 April 2026. Risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. Exploratory reconstruction was a secondary analysis. The study protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO with the following ID: CRD420261397950.
Three randomized controlled trials including 1156 patients were identified. Planned PCI was not associated with significant differences in all-cause mortality (risk ratio = 0.90, 95% CI = 0.70-1.15), trial-defined major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; risk ratio = 0.91, 95% CI = 0.70-1.18; supportive and exploratory because composite components differed), cardiovascular death (risk ratio = 0.74, 95% CI = 0.51-1.08), or myocardial infarction (risk ratio = 0.86, 95% CI = 0.45-1.63). It was associated with fewer urgent (risk ratio = 0.33, 95% CI = 0.13-0.87) and any subsequent revascularizations (risk ratio = 0.25, 95% CI = 0.07-0.87), but more trial-reported major bleeding (risk ratio = 1.57, 95% CI = 1.07-2.32; definitions varied) and any bleeding (risk ratio = 1.77, 95% CI = 1.27-2.47).
Routine planned PCI around TAVI was not shown to reduce mortality or major ischemic outcomes. It was associated with fewer subsequent revascularizations and more trial-reported major bleeding and any bleeding, supporting selective, individualized decision-making.

title: When History Returns: Hybrid Management of Syphilitic Aortitis Causing Severe Aortic Arch Branch Stenosis and Cerebral Hypoperfusion.
authors: Julia Al Mousli; Anders Håkanson; Jonas Malmstedt; David Lindström
abstract:
Cardiovascular manifestations of tertiary syphilis are rare in the antibiotic era, but important to consider in atypical vascular findings. These manifestations typically appear several years after the primary infection and may lead to structural damage in the cardiovascular system, requiring surgical intervention despite appropriate antibiotic therapy.
This case describes a rare manifestation of cardiovascular syphilis in a 46 year old woman presenting with dizziness, pre-syncope, and syncope consistent with global cerebral ischaemia. Extensive evaluation revealed syphilitic aortitis with severe stenosis and or occlusion of all the major aortic arch branches. The patient was managed with antibiotic therapy in combination with surgical revascularisation. Both endovascular and open surgical approaches were used to restore blood flow to the left common carotid, left vertebral, and left subclavian arteries. This intervention improved cerebral perfusion and resolved the patient's symptoms. At two years, the carotid stent was patent, while the carotid subclavian bypass was occluded. The patient remained free from cerebral ischaemic symptoms but reported bilateral arm claudication.
Tertiary syphilis should be considered as a differential diagnosis when atypical arterial disease is encountered. Hybrid revascularisation may provide an effective, less invasive treatment strategy.

title: Impact of True and False Lumen Origins on Target Vessel Instability in Post-Dissection F/BEVAR.
authors: Vivian C Gomes; Mark A Farber; Adam W Beck; Matthew J Eagleton; Gustavo S Oderich; Lucas R Kanamori; Bruno Schmid; Andres Schanzer; Matthew P Sweet; Sara L Zettervall; Carlos H Timaran; Xingsheng Li; Ryan S Cantor; F Ezequiel Parodi; U.S. Aortic Research Consortium
abstract:
To evaluate the occurrence of target artery-related adverse events in post-dissection F/BEVAR patients, based upon artery origin from the true or false lumen.
This is a multicenter, prospective, cohort study evaluating post-dissection patients treated with F/BEVAR, in the US Aortic Research Consortium. The primary endpoint was 5-year target vessel instability (TVI). Secondary endpoints included 5-year primary patency, freedom from secondary interventions (SIs), and type Ic and IIIc endoleaks. The analysis was performed on a per-vessel basis.
A total of 1052 target arteries were analyzed, primarily including the celiac, superior mesenteric, and renal arteries, with individual hepatic and splenic arteries occasionally incorporated in the repair. Of the 277 patients included, 75% were men, and 19% were black, with a mean age of 66.8 ± 10.3 years. The mean aneurysm sac diameter was 66.0 ± 11.4 mm, with extent II thoracoabdominal aneurysms being the most prevalent (72.6%) among this cohort. Technical success was obtained in 96% of the cases. As primary outcome, the incidence of target vessel instability (TVI) was significantly lower (P<0.001) among the true-lumen vessels (16.4%) compared to false-lumen (29.9%) and dual-lumen arteries (43.8%). As for the secondary outcomes, the incidence of type Ic endoleak was significantly higher (P=0.001) in false-lumen vessels (9.6%) and dual-lumen vessels (8.6%) compared to true-lumen vessels (3.3%). There was no significant difference in the incidence of type IIIc endoleak (p=0.241) or target vessel occlusion (P=0.458). Target artery stenosis was significantly more common among arteries originating from the false lumen compared to true lumen (2.6% vs 0.4%, P=0.009). Fenestrations were associated with a higher incidence (30.5%) of TVI when compared to branches (5.9% P=0.005), however, this was observed only among dual-lumen vessels. Arteries incorporated by a fenestration and that had a dual-lumen origin, were associated with a higher occurrence of secondary interventions (23.7%) compared to true-lumen vessels (8.6%, P=0.010). The same was not observed among the arteries incorporated by a branch configuration. The time-to-event analysis demonstrated a significantly higher 5-year freedom from TVI in true-lumen vessels compared to false and dual-lumen ones (True lumen: 83.6%; False=70.1 %; Dual=56.2 %; Log-rank P=0.0002). Freedom from secondary interventions at 5 years was significantly higher in true-lumen vessels compared to dual-lumen ones (Log-rank P=0.0104), but not to false-lumen arteries (Log-rank P=0.0847). The 5-year primary patency did not differ significantly among groups (True lumen: 98.3%; False = 92.6%; Dual=93.9%; Log-rank P=0.1368). On Cox proportional hazards analysis, dual-lumen (95% CI 1.24-3.28, p=0.005) and false-lumen (95% CI 1.04 - 2.60, p=0.0325) target arteries were associated with an increased hazard of TVI, when compared to true lumen arteries, having 2.02 (P=0.005) and 1.65 (P=0.0325) times more risk of presenting TVI than a true-lumen vessel CONCLUSIONS: In F/BEVAR for post-dissection aneurysms, target vessel instability and secondary intervention are significantly lower in target arteries originating from the true lumen, when compared to false-lumen or dual-lumen vessels. Device design, with use of fenestrations or branches may also play a role, with a significant difference only observed in dual-lumen target arteries.

title: Practical Solutions to Common TAVI Complications
authors: Herbert Kroon
abstract: Aortic valve stenosis Calcific aortic valve degeneration mainly affects the elderly population. Approximately 15% of elderly patients have some degree of aortic stenosis (AS)1. Untreated severe AS will lead to heart failure, angina and/or syncope and approximately half of patients will expire within 2 years after symptom onset1, 2. Historically, open heart surgery was the only treatment for severe AS. However, advanced age was a dominant argument to defer surgery. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) was contrived as a less invasive alternative to surgery and to fulfill this unmet clinical need. After the first-in-human procedure in 2002, TAVI matured into a guideline recommended treatment of symptomatic severe AS in elderly patients across the entire risk spectrum3-7. Peri-procedural embolization Operator experience, improved planning and implantation strategies and multiple device iterations including smaller profile, repositioning ability and outer sealing fabric converted TAVI into a reproducible and relatively safe procedure8. However, the “Big Five” of complications in the modern TAVI era remain 1) access site complications and bleedings, 2) paravalvular leakage (PVL), 3) acute kidney injury (AKI), 4) conduction disturbances including the need for permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) and 5) stroke9. Up to 5% of patients suffer a neurological event after TAVI, mainly within the first 48 hours8, 10, 11. This finding suggests a direct causative role with the transcatheter valve implantation itself. Transcranial Doppler and brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) studies revealed debris embolization towards the brain and new brain lesions after TAVI in the vast majority of patients12-15. Most of these embolizations remain clinically silent at first sight but may be linked to neurocognitive decline and frank dementia16. Embolic protection devices (EPD) have been developed to deflect or capture embolized debris on its way to the brain and may possibly reduce brain lesions and neurological events including stroke and neurocognitive decline. Part I of this thesis adds perspective to the etiopathology of TAVI related stroke and the mechanism of action of the current spectrum of cerebral embolic protection devices. We also present insights into the microscopic analysis of debris that was captured with filters during TAVI procedures. Vascular access and complications 1 TAVI typically requires large bore femoral artery access. By default, larger arteriotomies are at higher risk for access site complications and bleedings. A completely percutaneous approach relies on vascular access closure devices (VCD) to manage the arteriotomy and provide patent hemostasis. TAVI in low to intermediate risk patients is associated with a major vascular complication rate ranging between 2 and 8%4, 11. The conventional closure technique is based on sutures and most access site complications after TAVI procedures are related to closure device failure17. A collagen plug based closure device was introduced as an alternative to sutures. Part II of this thesis addresses vascular complications and provides information on clinical outcomes with collagen plug-based VCD. TAVI-related conduction disturbances Acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI are frequent and may lead to heart failure (re-) admissions and impaired long-term prognosis18-22. The atrioventricular bundle pierces the membranous septum between the right and non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve and surfaces along the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), which makes it vulnerable to contact pressure by the implanted transcatheter heart valve (THV) during TAVI23, 24. New left bundle branch block (LBBB) and third-degree atrioventricular block (AV3B) requiring PPI occur in up to a third and quarter of patients, respectively18-22. These conduction disturbances may be transient or remain permanent which is clinically relevant in view of in-hospital stay and overall healthcare costs. Unfortunately, there are no uniform definitions to describe conduction dynamics post-TAVI. Inconsistent reporting makes the interpretation of the literature on this topic challenging. Part III of this thesis will elaborate on what is currently known about the incidence of newly acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI and studies specific features on the baseline and postprocedural electrocardiogram (ECG) to predict conduction dynamics. These insights may help determine the need and timing of PPI and adjust hospital discharge policies.

title: Impact of cardiac phase selection on the diagnostic performance of CT-FFR: the role of myocardial bridging and heart rate
authors: Jianhui Song; Jie Zhou; QIYU ZHANG; FANG ZHANG; WEI GAO; YAN XIA; J Y Ma; Rende Xu; LEILEI MA; JUYING QIAN; CHENGUANG LI; JUNBO GE
abstract: Abstract Background Computed tomography-derived fractional flow reserve (CT-FFR) is a promising non-invasive tool, but the reliability of the conventionally preferred diastolic phase is challenged by high heart rates or myocardial bridging. This study aimed to compare the diagnostic performance of systolic versus diastolic CT-FFR to identify the optimal reconstruction phase based on patient-specific characteristics. Methods This retrospective study analyzed 155 vessel segments from 138 patients with suspected coronary artery disease undergoing coronary CT angiography and invasive FFR. CT-FFR was calculated in diastolic and systolic phases. Diagnostic accuracy was assessed against invasive FFR (≤ 0.80 as positive), with stratified analyses for the FFR grey zone (0.75–0.85), myocardial bridging, and heart rate (≤ 70 vs > 70 beats per minute). Results Among 138 patients (mean age 65.4 ± 9.8 years; 91 men), diastolic CT-FFR demonstrated superior overall performance (AUC 0.91 vs 0.87; P = 0.021). In the FFR grey zone, systolic CT-FFR showed lower specificity (52.8% vs 77.8%; P < 0.05). In myocardial bridging patients, systolic CT-FFR had significantly lower AUC (0.79 vs 0.90; P = 0.011). In patients with heart rates > 70 bpm, systolic CT-FFR showed numerically higher but non-significant performance (AUC 0.87 vs 0.85; P = 0.418). Conclusions The optimal cardiac phase for CT-FFR is patient-dependent. While diastole remains superior for the general population and critical for patients with myocardial bridging or borderline lesions, the systolic phase may provide a viable alternative for patients with high heart rates when imaged on single-source CT platforms. An individualized cardiac phase-selection strategy is recommended to optimize the diagnostic accuracy of CT-FFR.

title: Involvement of TRPC6/NFAT axis and mitochondrial quality control in the protective effect of aerobic exercise against doxorubicin-induced cardiomyopathy
authors: Wenjing Yi; Gao Yi-qian; Junwei Zhang; Huan-Huan Zhang; Bin Zheng; Jian-Feng Jiang; Meng-Ge Yao; Hai-Xia Jiao; Rui-Xing Wang; Long‐Xin Gui; Mo-Jun Lin; Rui‐Lan He; Minxia Wu; Zhijuan Wu
abstract: Doxorubicin (DOX), a common chemotherapeutic agent, leads to irreversible anthracycline-induced cardiomyopathy (AIC). Impaired mitochondrial quality control serves as a central pathogenic driver of AIC. Moreover, DOX provokes sustained overactivation of the TRPC6/NFAT cascade, generating self-amplifying excitation-transcription feedback in injured cardiomyocytes. Despite the well-documented cardioprotective potential of aerobic exercise, the causal interplay between TRPC6/NFAT signaling and mitochondrial homeostasis underlying this protection remains unclear. Male C57BL/6 J mice were randomly assigned to five groups with bidirectional pharmacological manipulation of TRPC6/NFAT activity: control, DOX, exercise + DOX, exercise + DOX + TRPC6 agonist hyperforin, and DOX + TRPC6 antagonist larixyl acetate. Aerobic exercise suppressed TRPC6/NFAT3 overactivation. This inhibition further normalized mitochondrial quality control by enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis, limiting excessive mitochondrial fission and suppressing excessive PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy signaling. The improvement in mitochondrial homeostasis was accompanied by attenuated DOX-induced myocardial injury, hypertrophy, and interstitial fibrosis. Echocardiography revealed restored systolic function with elevated left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and fractional shortening (LVFS). Treadmill testing further revealed recovered heart rate recovery (HRR), along with a longer exhaustive running distance and exercise duration. Notably, larixyl acetate recapitulated all exercise-conferred cardiac benefits, whereas hyperforin-mediated TRPC6/NFAT activation completely abrogated exercise-induced protection. In summary, aerobic exercise alleviates DOX-induced cardiomyopathy by disrupting the TRPC6/NFAT3 positive-feedback loop to restore mitochondrial quality control. This cascade of effects mitigates pathological myocardial remodeling, rescues left ventricular systolic performance, and increases systemic exercise tolerance, providing experimental evidence supporting exercise rehabilitation for patients with AIC.

title: Moderate Aortic Stenosis: Pathophysiology, Diagnostic Criteria, Prognosis and Evolving Management
authors: Niall Patrick Connolly; Jack Hartnett; Stephen O’Connor; Mark Hensey; Caroline Daly; Rose Anne Kenny; Andrew O Maree
abstract: Aortic stenosis (AS) is a progressive valvular disease with rising incidence, particularly among elderly populations. Although excess mortality in severe AS is well recognised, moderate AS is also associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Current guidelines recommend valve replacement only for severe AS or in moderate AS with a concomitant surgical indication, leaving a therapeutic gap. This review summarises current knowledge on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, natural history and diagnostic challenges of AS management, with an emphasis on moderate disease. We discuss prognostic markers, including myocardial fibrosis, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, global longitudinal strain and autonomic dysfunction, that may identify high-risk moderate AS patients. Evidence from recent and ongoing trials of transcatheter aortic valve replacement and novel pharmacotherapies is summarised, and limitations of existing valve prostheses and medical therapies are discussed. Improved risk stratification, earlier detection of pathological changes and targeted intervention may ultimately improve the management paradigm for moderate AS.

title: Perioperative outcomes after aortic valve replacement via right anterior mini-thoracotomy with a rapid-deployment valve: a consecutive single-centre series
authors: Łukasz Jaworski; Krzysztof Jarmoszewicz; Marian Burysz; Sebastian Batkiewicz; Adam Ryszard Kowalówka; Michał Kuteń
abstract: Background/objectives Evidence for aortic valve replacement through right anterior thoracotomy (RAT) using the Edwards Intuity Elite rapid-deployment bioprosthesis remains limited, with only three dedicated single-centre series published to date. We aimed to describe perioperative safety, early haemodynamic performance, permanent pacemaker implantation for third-degree atrioventricular block, and new-onset postoperative atrial fibrillation in a consecutive single-centre cohort. Analyses of factors associated with these two rhythm endpoints were exploratory in nature. Methods This is a retrospective, single-arm, single-centre observational series with no sternotomy, ministernotomy or sutured-valve comparator. We analysed 70 consecutive patients undergoing isolated aortic valve replacement via RAT with the Edwards Intuity Elite bioprosthesis at a single institution. Percutaneous femoral arterial and venous cannulation was used in all cases. Outcomes were described for the whole cohort. For exploratory event-versus-no-event comparisons, Mann–Whitney U and Fisher's exact tests were applied to permanent pacemaker implantation and new-onset atrial fibrillation; Spearman rank correlation and Mann–Whitney U tests explored associations with operative times and discharge pressure gradients. Because only 6 pacemaker and 7 atrial fibrillation events occurred, statistical power was limited. Results Median age was 71.0 years and median EuroSCORE II was 1.0%. Median cross-clamp time was 61.0 min (IQR 54–75) and median cardiopulmonary bypass time was 103.5 min (IQR 84–115). In-hospital mortality was 1.4% (one death from femoral cannulation-site haemorrhage; 95% CI 0.0%–7.7%), and no strokes occurred. Permanent pacemaker implantation was required in 6 patients (8.6%; 95% CI 3.2–17.7%) and new-onset atrial fibrillation occurred in 7 (10.0%; 95% CI 4.1–19.5%); age was significantly associated with pacemaker implantation (median 75.5 vs. 71.0 years, p = 0.038), while other exploratory comparisons were not significant. No moderate or severe paravalvular leak was observed. Median postoperative mean gradient was 8.0 mmHg (IQR 6–10) and median length of stay was 6.0 days (IQR 6.0–7.0). Packed red blood cell transfusion was required in 63 patients (91.3% of 69 evaluable; 95% CI 82.0–96.7%), and reoperation for bleeding in 3 (4.3%; 95% CI 0.9–12.0%). Exploratory analyses detected no statistically significant association with atrial fibrillation or operative times. Implanted valve size correlated weakly and inversely with postoperative mean gradient (Spearman rho = −0.26, p = 0.032). Conclusions In this descriptive, low-risk, single-centre cohort, RAT with a rapid-deployment bioprosthesis was feasible and was followed by low discharge gradients. The observed pacemaker, atrial fibrillation, transfusion, bleeding and access-site event rates are real-world descriptive estimates and do not constitute comparative evidence of benefit over other approaches or prostheses. The small number of events precludes conclusions about predictors. Larger prospective multicentre studies with comparator groups and systematic echocardiographic follow-up are required.

title: Application of abdominal CT radiomic features for discriminating prevalent coronary heart disease in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus
authors: He Sui; Yingchun Wan; Ming Qu; Yun Zhang; Xu Sun; Tao Li; Lin Liu; Zhanhao Mo
abstract: Purpose To develop and validate a hybrid model combining pancreatic-aortic radiomic features from non-contrast abdominal CT with clinical factors for discriminating prevalent coronary heart disease (CHD) status in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Materials and methods This retrospective study enrolled 407 T2DM patients (277 with CHD, 130 without), randomly split into training (n = 284) and internal test (n = 123) sets. Pancreatic auto-segmentation used a 3D V-Net, while the abdominal aortic wall was manually segmented by blinded radiologists. Following Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI)-compliant preprocessing, radiomic features underwent reproducibility filtering, collinearity removal, LASSO regression and coefficient threshold filtering (|β|>0.05). Five models were built using logistic regression, support vector machine and Gaussian process classifiers. Model performance was assessed by AUC, calibration plots and decision-curve analysis (DCA). Results Seven pancreatic, nine aortic and three combined radiomic features were retained. The hybrid model yielded a numerically higher test-set AUC of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.77–0.91). Its discriminative performance was numerically greater than the clinical model (AUC = 0.65, 95% CI: 0.56–0.74; P < 0.001), pancreatic radiomic model (AUC = 0.70), aortic radiomic model (AUC = 0.82), and combined radiomic model (AUC = 0.83). It exhibited favorable calibration, with a net clinical benefit comparable to or numerically greater than the alternative models across threshold probabilities of 10%–90% on DCA. Conclusion The hybrid clinical-radiomic model improves discrimination of prevalent CHD status in T2DM patients, supporting opportunistic non-invasive identification of existing CHD using routine non-contrast abdominal CT.

title: Clinical cardiovascular impact of valvular heart disease subtypes in chronic hemodialysis patients
authors: Wan‐Lun Hsu; Vy-Khanh Nguyen; Yukiko Ono; Chung‐Kuan Wu
abstract: Valvular heart disease (VHD) is highly prevalent in patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) undergoing hemodialysis (HD), and is linked to adverse cardiovascular outcomes. However, data remain limited regarding its prognosis impact across different types of VHD in the population. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 238 chronic HD patients with echocardiographic assessments at a single medical center. VHD was identified and classified by lesion types and number of affected valves (isolated vs. multivalvular). Clinical outcomes included all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and cardiovascular mortality. Cox proportional hazards models and Kaplan-Meier analyses were used for analysis. VHD was present in 87.4% of the cohort, with mitral regurgitation (MR) being the most common (91.3%), followed by aortic regurgitation (48.6%), aortic stenosis (13.0%), and mitral stenosis (1.4%). VHD patients were older and had higher coronary artery disease prevalence. Although VHD presence was not significantly associated with adverse outcomes in multivariable models, Kaplan-Meier analysis showed higher event trends (MACE: 38% vs. 20%; CV mortality: 18.3% vs. 6.7%). Subgroup analysis revealed that aortic stenosis (AS) was significantly associated with increased MACE risk (adjusted HR: 1.919; 95% CI: 1.065–3.548), and exploratory analyses suggested MR might be associated with all-cause mortality (adjusted HR: 2.538; 95% CI: 1.000–6.446). While overall VHD presence was not independently predictive of adverse outcomes, exploratory analyses identified potential associations between specific valvular lesions, such as AS and MR, and adverse clinical outcomes, emphasizing the need for further VHD subtype evaluation and risk stratification in chronic HD population.

title: Associations between circulating inflammatory markers and left ventricular systolic function in liver transplant recipients
authors: Sofie Larsen Øland; Ask Bock; Jens Hillingsø; Nicoline Arentoft; Thomas R. Holtveg; Anne Jensen; Emilie Høegholm Ernst Lauridsen; Henning Grønbæk; Peter Holland-Fischer; Annette Dam Fialla; Jens Otto Clemmesen; Jesper J. Linde; Hans-Christian Pommergaard; Tor Biering-Sørensen; Susanne Dam Nielsen
abstract: Introduction Cardiovascular disease, including heart failure, is one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality among liver transplant recipients. Inflammatory markers are associated with heart failure in the general population. We aimed to assess whether high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), interleukin (IL)-6, and soluble (s)CD163 were associated with left ventricular (LV) systolic function in liver transplant recipients. Methods In this cross-sectional study adult liver transplant recipients from the Danish Comorbidity in Liver Transplant Recipients (DACOLT) study who underwent research transthoracic echocardiography and measurements of hs-CRP, IL-6, and sCD163 were included. Outcomes were LV global longitudinal strain (LV GLS), LV ejection fraction (LVEF), and LV systolic dysfunction, defined as LV GLS <16% and/or LVEF <50%. Results We included 317 participants. Median LV GLS was 18.4% (IQR: 16.4-20.1), median LVEF was 54.0% (IQR: 50.0-57.0), and the prevalence of LV systolic dysfunction was 31.5%. In unadjusted analyses, each doubling of hs-CRP, IL-6, and sCD163 were associated with lower LV GLS with associations of -0.29% (95% CI: [-0.50; -0.08], p=0.008), -0.38% (95% CI: [-0.63; -0.13], p=0.003), and -0.37% (95% CI: [-0.73; -0.02], p=0.041), respectively. Associations with LVEF in unadjusted analyses were -0.61% (95% CI: [-1.02; -0.20], p=0.004), -0.86% (95% CI: [-1.34; -0.38], p=0.001), and -0.37% (95% CI: [-1.07;0.33], p=0.297) per doubling of hs-CRP, IL-6 and sCD163, respectively. However, in models adjusting for sex, age, BMI, and smoking status these associations were attenuated. Conclusion Higher levels of the circulating inflammatory markers hs-CRP, IL-6, and sCD163 were associated with LV systolic function in liver transplant recipients. However, these associations were attenuated in adjusted analyses and thus seem to be explained by traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether inflammatory markers can improve risk stratification and identify those at increased risk of LV systolic dysfunction and heart failure. Clinical trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov , identifier NCT04777032.

title: Measurement of Ankle Brachial Pressure Index in Diabetic Patients and Diabetic Foot Ulcer Patients and its Value to Assess the Degree of Ischemia in Peripheral Arterial Disease
authors: D. Monisha Devi; S. Padma; S.K. Manoj; Vinoth Kanna D; N. Sathish; M. Malathi; P. Karthick
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
abstract: Background: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are a common and severe illness frequently linked to peripheral artery disease (PAD), resulting in compromised wound healing and increased vulnerability to infection and necrosis. The Ankle–Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) is an easy, non-invasive instrument utilized to assess peripheral artery circulation. This study intended to examine the Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) values of diabetic patients with and without foot ulcers, as well as to evaluate vascular insufficiency in patients with diabetic foot ulcers using the ABPI and Doppler. Material and Methods: A comparative observational study was done among patients with Diabetic foot ulcers (n = 45) and patients without foot ulcers (n = 45). Their Ankle Brachial Pressure Index was measured, and they were subjected to Doppler ultrasonography. A comparative analysis was carried out among both groups Results: The average ABPI for patients with diabetic foot ulcers was 1.018 ± 0.2949, while diabetic patients without ulcers exhibited a significantly elevated average ABPI of 1.216 ± 0.1107. Doppler waveform analysis indicated that 40.00% of diabetic foot ulcer patients displayed a biphasic waveform, 31.11% exhibited a triphasic waveform, and 28.88% presented a monophasic waveform. Conversely, among patients devoid of ulcers, 91.11% exhibited a triphasic waveform, 8.88% displayed a biphasic waveform, and none presented a monophasic flow. Conclusion: The research indicates that diabetic individuals with foot ulcers exhibit notably reduced ABPI values and a higher prevalence of abnormal Doppler waveform patterns in comparison to patients without ulcers. Lower ABPI values and monophasic Doppler waveforms exhibit a significant correlation with peripheral arterial disease in patients with diabetic foot ulcers. The combination of ABPI and Doppler ultrasonography represents a reliable, non-invasive approach for the early identification of vascular insufficiency in diabetic patients.

title: Comparison of unilateral monitoring and bilateral monitoring for detection of right-to-left shunt by contrast-enhanced transcranial Doppler: a two-center retrospective study
authors: Liebiao Peng; Qiaomin Zhang; Pengbo Gao; 张维君
abstract: Background Contrast-enhanced Transcranial Doppler (c-TCD) can identify high-risk right-to-left shunt (RLS) through the quantification of the shunt. But the difference of monitoring methods may result in important disagreements regarding the outcomes of c-TCD assessments. The aim of the study is to establish whether c-TCD with unilateral monitoring is as effective as bilateral monitoring for the detection of RLS. Methods A two-center retrospective study was conducted. 249 patients underwent c-TCD examination by monitoring bilateral middle cerebral arteries. The differences in diagnostic yield and shunt extents between unilateral monitoring and bilateral monitoring were mainly compared. Results There was no significant difference in diagnostic yield between unilateral monitoring and bilateral monitoring. There was significant difference in shunt extents between unilateral monitoring and bilateral monitoring, primarily concentrated in low-grade shunts, while completely consistent in moderate-to-large shunts. Conclusion While overall detection rates are similar between unilateral and bilateral monitoring, the main difference lies in reclassification of low-grade shunts, whereas concordance remains high for moderate-to-large shunts. Monitoring methods can be selected to play complementary roles according to the clinical objective (screening or phenotype).

title: New onset atrial fibrillation after transcatheter aortic valve implantation in Southwestern Colombia between 2009 and 2023
authors: John Fernando Montenegro-Palacios; Diana Marcela Bonilla; Antonio Dager; Jhon Quintana; Carlos Andrés Cardona; Nelson Murillo; yamil liscano; Jhony Alejandro Díaz-Vallejo; Jamil Cedillo-Balcázar; Mario Valladares Garrido
abstract: Background New-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) is an important complication after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Methods This retrospective cohort included 218 patients without documented pre-existing atrial fibrillation who underwent TAVI in Cali, Colombia, between 2009 and 2023. NOAF required an electrocardiographically documented episode lasting at least 30 s within 30 days. Clinical surveillance included inpatient telemetry and ECGs, scheduled follow-up and institutional readmissions; individual follow-up completeness was not quantified. We compared categorical characteristics and performed a sensitivity analysis restricted to recorded severe or critical aortic stenosis. Results NOAF was documented in 44/218 patients (20.2%; 95% CI, 15.4–26.0%). In the restricted subset, 35/164 had documented NOAF (21.3%; 95% CI, 15.8–28.2%). Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease was more frequent among patients with NOAF (61.4% versus 31.0%; unadjusted OR, 3.53; 95% CI, 1.78–7.01). Pacemaker implantation and low-molecular-weight heparin use were also more frequent in that group, describing perioperative co-occurrence. Conclusion Approximately one-fifth of patients had NOAF documented in the available records. Restriction to recorded severe or critical stenosis produced a similar frequency. The estimate describes clinical documentation within a 30-day window and requires interpretation in light of incomplete ascertainment and indication verification.

title: Regulatory roles of microRNA‑145 in cardiovascular diseases (Review)
authors: Ruo-Han Jian; Sen Huang
abstract: MicroRNA‑145 (miR‑145) is a non‑coding RNA involved in vascular remodeling, myocardial injury and fibrosis, and it contributes to the onset and progression of several cardiovascular disorders. Accumulating evidence indicates that the functions of miR‑145 depend on cell subtypes and pathological microenvironments. miR‑145 exerts dual regulatory effects in atherosclerosis, myocardial ischemia‑reperfusion injury, hypertension, pulmonary arterial hypertension ventricular remodeling and heart failure. In some settings, for example in cardiomyocytes subjected to myocardial ischemia‑reperfusion injury (MIRI), miR‑145 can suppress disease progression and protect the myocardium and vasculature; conversely, it may trigger tissue injury and exacerbate disease in specific cell types and pathological setting; for example, in cardiac microvascular endothelial cells during MIRI. Abnormal expression of miR‑145 is associated with disease severity, risk stratification and the incidence of long‑term adverse cardiovascular events, suggesting its potential as a molecular biomarker for early screening, disease assessment and prognosis of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). Unconjugated or unformulated miR is limited by poor in vivo stability, rapid degradation by ribonucleases and low cellular transfection efficiency. To address these limitations, three major delivery platforms, namely extracellular vesicles, viral vectors and nanoparticles, have been developed for targeted delivery of miR‑145 and these platforms differ in biosafety, delivery efficacy and modifiability. As research advances in nucleic acid‑based targeted therapeutics, several miR‑based agents have entered clinical trials, supporting the development of targeted interventions for CVDs. The present review examined the dual regulatory mechanisms, potential clinical applications and current delivery technologies of miR‑145 across CVDs. The translational progress and limitations of current miR therapeutics were reviewed, as well as unresolved controversies and unanswered scientific questions. The present work aimed to inform further mechanistic studies of miR‑145 and the research, development and clinical translation of cardiovascular nucleic acid‑targeted therapies.

title: Heart Failure Beyond Valve Treatment ― Mechanisms, Predictors, and Therapeutic Strategies After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement ―
authors: Hideki Kitahara; Kaoru Matsuura; Yoshio Kobayashi
abstract: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has become an established treatment for severe aortic stenosis across the spectrum of surgical risk, substantially improving symptoms and clinical outcomes. However, heart failure (HF) remains a major cause of hospitalization and mortality after TAVR, indicating that relief of valvular stenosis alone may not completely eliminate HF risk. HF after TAVR is multifactorial, reflecting residual cardiac damage and incomplete reverse remodeling, concomitant cardiovascular abnormalities, procedure- and prosthesis-related factors, underlying HF substrate, and systemic comorbidities. Importantly, both the baseline extent of cardiac damage and its persistence after TAVR are associated with adverse outcomes, highlighting the importance of serial assessment beyond procedural success. In addition, many patients undergoing TAVR are elderly and have features of HF with preserved ejection fraction, which may contribute to persistent HF despite successful valve intervention. Emerging evidence, including randomized trial data on sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, suggests that targeted pharmacological therapy may reduce residual HF risk after TAVR. In this review we summarize the epidemiology, clinical impact, mechanisms, risk stratification, and management of HF after TAVR, and discuss future strategies for its prevention and treatment.

title: Navigating Severe Aortic Stenosis in Hip Fracture Surgery: Perioperative Management and Surgical Timing
authors: Richard Bui; Jen Li Dong; Austin Tran; Laasya Achanta; Jamal Hasoon; Alaa Abd-Elsayed; Alan David Kaye; Anvinh Nguyen
abstract: Severe aortic stenosis presents a significant challenge in patients requiring urgent hip fracture surgery. Although aortic stenosis increases the risk of cardiovascular complications and mortality, delaying fixation may independently contribute to morbidity, functional decline, and mortality. This creates a dilemma regarding whether to proceed directly to surgery or delay fracture repair for aortic valve intervention. This review examines management of patients with severe aortic stenosis pending urgent hip fracture surgery, with emphasis on timing, preoperative evaluation, anesthetic selection, and hemodynamic management. Current evidence suggests that asymptomatic patients with preserved left ventricular systolic function and stable hemodynamics may often undergo timely fracture fixation with appropriate monitoring. In contrast, symptomatic patients, those with ventricular dysfunction or hemodynamic instability, and patients with particularly severe disease may require evaluation for valvular intervention. When intervention is indicated, transcatheter aortic valve replacement may offer a more rapid treatment in certain patients, while balloon aortic valvuloplasty may serve as a temporizing strategy. For patients proceeding directly to fracture fixation, preservation of preload, systemic vascular resistance, coronary perfusion, and sinus rhythm is essential. Current evidence does not establish a clear superiority of general versus neuraxial anesthesia, supporting individualized anesthetic planning and avoidance of abrupt hemodynamic changes. Ultimately, management should balance the risks of delaying fracture fixation against the risks of surgery through coordinated, multidisciplinary decision-making.

title: Controlled hypotension in anesthesia: Principles, applications, and perioperative considerations
authors: Adel Botros; Farahat Ibrahim Ahmed; Mohamed Ibrahim Ramadan Ismail ElAtfy; Ayman Eskander Tawfeek
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
abstract: Controlled hypotension or hypotensive anesthesia is an anesthetic technique used to intentionally reduce arterial blood pressure in order to minimize intraoperative blood loss with subsequent decreasing the requirements of blood transfusion an/or improving surgical field visibility with subsequent meticulous surgical dissection and shortening of surgery time This technique has been frequently applied in surgical procedures associated with significant bleeding, particularly neurosurgical maxillofacial, spinal, orthopedic, otolaryngologic, plastic and endoscopic sinus surgeries. The technique can be achieved through pharmacological method via using various specific hypotensive pharmacological agents and non pharmacological method via various maneuvers as patient head up positioning, high level neuraxial block , and deepening of general anesthesia,. The decision to induce hypotensive anesthesia should be based according to the patient's general condition, the extent of the surgery, and in coordination with the operating surgeon. The target blood pressure should be adjusted according to the patient’s preoperative status and coexisting illness. The risk of organ hypoperfusion should be kept in mind. Understanding the physiological basis of controlled hypotension, available techniques, and pharmacological agents used for induced hypotension, careful patient selection and close monitoring with adequate intraoperative volume replacement are mandatory for its safe implementation in surgical cases. The aim of this review article is to through the light on the physiological basis of controlled hypotension, its indications, contraindications, the commonly used techniques, and the potential associated complications.

title: Valve Embolisation During Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation (TAVI): Clinical Outcomes and CT-Derived Anatomical Characteristics
authors: Dominic Dalip; Amerjeet Banning; Raj Rajendra
abstract: Background Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has transformed the management of severe aortic stenosis, offering an effective alternative for elderly patients and those at high surgical risk who are not ideal candidates for open-heart surgery. Of late, there is an expansion into intermediate- and low-risk populations as well. Transcatheter valve embolisation or migration (TVEM) is a rare but potentially fatal complication. Predictors of TVEM are incompletely understood, and there is a gap in evidence, looking specifically at the CT-derived anatomical characteristics of TVEM. Aim This study aimed to quantify the incidence of TVEM in a high-volume tertiary centre and characterise anatomical patterns in patients experiencing TVEM during TAVI. Methods This is a retrospective, single-centre study. Patients registered as having TVEM were identified using the local database from June 2014 to June 2024. Case notes of these patients were then studied to assess the management of TVEM and outcomes. For this cohort of patients, preprocedural CTs were analysed in detail, including annulus perimeter and area, qualitative leaflet calcification grading (moderate, severe, very severe), presence of annular/aorto-mitral curtain (AMC) calcification, and minimum sinus of Valsalva (SOV) diameter. Procedural data included initial embolised valve type and the bailout strategy. Results The incidence of TVEM was 0.51% with a 30-day mortality of 40% and average length of stay in hospital of 11.5 days, compared with the uncomplicated TAVI length of stay averaging 2.1 days. There was a periprocedural complication of stroke in 10% of patients (1 patient) and no vascular access site complication. Leaflet calcification was severe or very severe in 9/10 patients, with AMC calcification present in half. The mean minimum SOV diameter was 28.7 +/- 3.5 mm (23-34 mm), and several cases demonstrated markedly constrained aortic root anatomy. All embolised valves were self-expanding devices. In 4/10 cases, a balloon-expandable THV was used as the second device, while 6/10 were treated with another self-expanding THV. Conclusion Findings suggest that TVEM is a rare complication associated with substantial short-term mortality. Severe leaflet calcification, AMC calcification, and smaller SOV dimensions were frequently observed in this cohort, and all embolised valves were self-expanding. These findings are descriptive and hypothesis-generating; without a comparator group, their association with embolisation risk cannot be established. However, these anatomical findings warrant careful preprocedural assessment, while prospective comparative studies are needed to determine their association with TVEM risk.

title: Carotid CTA with automated plaque quantification for risk stratification of coexisting obstructive coronary artery disease
authors: Long Jiang Zhang; Minjie Zhao; Changsheng Zhou; JiaNan Li; Sijia Zhao; Jing Li; Hao Tang; Sui Chen; Rui Liu; Wusheng Zhu; Ya Liu; Yun Zhang; 啓吉 金; Wenjing Cui; Pengbo Jiang; Dijia Wu; Xiaoqing Cheng; Zhang Longjiang
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether automated carotid plaque quantification on carotid computed tomography angiography (CTA) can serve as an adjunctive risk stratification tool for identifying patients with coexisting obstructive coronary artery disease (OCAD). MATERIALS AND METHODS: This dual-center retrospective study included 2533 adults undergoing paired carotid and coronary CTA within 3 months. Carotid plaque components (calcified, fibrotic, and lipid) were quantified automatically. In the modeling cohort, three diagnostic models for OCAD (stenosis ≥ 50%) were developed using LASSO regression: clinical, plaque, and integrated models. Performance was assessed by AUC (with DeLong's test), decision curve analysis, and calibration curves, with validation in an internal validation set and a temporally independent validation cohort. Sensitivity analysis was performed using severe stenosis (≥ 70%) as the outcome. RESULTS: All carotid plaque volumes were significantly associated with OCAD (p < 0.001). Calcified plaque volume (OR, 2.43; 95% CI: 1.95-3.04) and fibrotic plaque volume (OR, 1.37; 95% CI: 1.01-1.85) were independent predictors. The plaque model achieved an AUC of 0.785 (95% CI: 0.761-0.810) in the training set, comparable to the integrated model (AUC, 0.800) and superior to the clinical model (AUC, 0.723; p < 0.001). Performance remained robust in the internal (AUC, 0.824) and external validation set (AUC, 0.813). The integrated model demonstrated good calibration. Sensitivity analysis yielded consistent results. CONCLUSION: In this retrospective study, automated carotid plaque quantification on CTA provides an adjunctive risk stratification tool to identify patients at high risk for coexisting OCAD, potentially guiding decisions regarding downstream coronary examinations. KEY POINTS: Question Quantitative analysis of carotid plaque components on CTA may help identify patients with OCAD. Findings A model integrating automated carotid plaque volumes and clinical factors effectively identified OCAD. Clinical Relevance This study demonstrates that automated carotid plaque quantification on CTA may serve as an adjunctive risk stratification tool to guide downstream coronary testing in patients with cerebrovascular disease.

title: N-acetylcysteine rescues intracellular Ca2+ signalling and nitric oxide production in human aortic valve endothelial cells from patients with calcific aortic valve stenosis
authors: Pawan Sirwan Faris; Vincenza Valerio; Ilaria Massaiu; Sharon Negri; Giorgia Scarpellino; Valentina Brunetti; Veronika A. Myasoedova; Paolo Poggio; Francesco Domenico Moccia
abstract: Calcific aortic valve stenosis (CAVS), the most common valvular heart disease, is generally regarded as a progressive disease continuum evolving from aortic valve sclerosis (AVSc) to overt aortic stenosis (AS), characterized by increasing leaflet calcification and outflow obstruction. Endothelial dysfunction of the aortic valve plays a crucial role in the pathogenic mechanism leading to CAVS. A remarkable increase in oxidative stress contributes to endothelial injury in CAVS, thereby promoting endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition and impairing endothelium-dependent vasomotion and endothelial barrier function. Endothelial dysfunction can be accompanied by remodelling of the Ca 2+ handling machinery and restoring intracellular Ca 2+ signalling could represent a promising therapeutic strategy to recover endothelial function, including nitric oxide (NO) release. We adopted a multidisciplinary approach (i.e., RNA-seq analysis of Ca²⁺ toolkit-associated genes and single-cell Fura-2 Ca 2+ imaging for intracellular measurements) to investigate for the first time whether the Ca 2+ signalling toolkit is altered in human aortic valve endothelial cells (hVECs) from patients with CAVS (AS-hVECs) compared to VECs from control patients (hVECs; i.e., isolated from patients without stenosis). Bioinformatic analysis revealed that the transcripts encoding inositol-1,4,5-trisphosphate (InsP 3 ) receptors (InsP 3 Rs), i.e., ITPR1 , ITPR2 , and ITPR3 , which mediate Ca 2+ release from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), were not altered, while the transcript encoding the ER Ca 2+ sensor STIM1, which initiates store-operated Ca 2+ entry (SOCE), was up-regulated in AS-hVECs. Capillary Western blot revealed that InsP 3 R and STIM1, but not Orai1 (the main pore-forming subunit of SOCE), proteins were significantly over-expressed in AS-hVECs. Unexpectedly, single-cell Fura-2 Ca 2+ imaging revealed that SOCE, a major driver of endothelial NO release, was remarkably down-regulated in AS-hVECs. Conversely, despite a reduction in the amount of releasable free ER Ca 2+ , physiological Ca 2+ release through InsP 3 Rs was unaffected, reflecting InsP 3 R hyper-responsiveness in AS-hVECs. However, N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC), a widely employed ROS scavenger, and the thiol-reducing agent dithiothreitol (DTT) fully rescued SOCE, consistent with the ROS-dependent inhibition of SOCE activation. Furthermore, pre-treatment with NAC also restored acetylcholine-induced NO release. These findings reveal that oxidative stress impairs SOCE in AS-hVECs and identify NAC as a potential therapeutic strategy to prevent endothelial dysfunction in this heart valve disease.

title: Presumed True Inferior Epigastric Artery Aneurysm Associated with External Iliac Artery Stenosis Treated with Coil Embolization
authors: Yu Masuda; Hiroki Higashihara; Takahiro Nakagawa; Taro Yamasumi; Keisuke Miyake; Yusuke Ono; Noriyuki Tomiyama
abstract: A 77-year-old man underwent contrast-enhanced computed tomography before transcatheter aortic valve implantation, revealing severe stenosis of the right external iliac artery and an 8 × 9 × 28 mm presumed true inferior epigastric artery aneurysm at its anastomosis with the obturator artery. Comparison with prior computed tomography images demonstrated aneurysmal enlargement, and endovascular coil embolization was therefore performed because of concern for rupture. Pelvic angiography demonstrated multiple collateral pathways supplying the right lower extremity, and coil embolization was performed after multidisciplinary assessment. Complete embolization of the aneurysm and parent artery was achieved using 11 detachable coils, with no postprocedural claudication. This extremely rare case of aneurysmal degeneration in lower-extremity collateral circulation highlights the importance of evaluating collateral pathways and limb ischemia risk before embolization.

title: Recurrent prosthetic valve endocarditis with suspected perivalvular abscess caused by Staphylococcus caprae in a bone marrow transplant recipient: a case report
authors: Tomohiro Nakajima; Yutaka Iba; Tsuyoshi Shibata; Junji Nakazawa; Hidemichi Kouzu; Satoshi Iyama
abstract: Abstract Background Infective endocarditis (IE) in bone marrow transplantation (BMT) recipients is uncommon but carries high mortality. Recurrent prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) in immunocompromised hosts presents particular challenges in surgical decision-making. Staphylococcus caprae , a coagulase-negative staphylococcus of caprine origin, is rarely implicated in human IE. We report a rare case of recurrent S. caprae PVE with suspected perivalvular abscess in a BMT recipient managed with advance care planning (ACP) and home-based palliative care. Case presentation A 63-year-old male had undergone allogeneic BMT for high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and was receiving immunosuppression for chronic graft-versus-host disease. Approximately 13 months after BMT, he developed cardiogenic shock due to S. caprae IE causing severe aortic regurgitation and underwent emergency aortic valve replacement (AVR) with a 27-mm INSPIRIS RESILIA bioprosthesis (Edwards Lifesciences) and concomitant coronary artery bypass grafting. The initial event has been previously reported. Approximately eight weeks after completion of a 42-day antimicrobial course, he was readmitted with fever and rigors, and blood cultures again grew S. caprae with an antimicrobial susceptibility profile indistinguishable from that of the index isolate; strain-level molecular typing was not performed. Transesophageal echocardiography approximately one month later showed an isoechoic structure at the subaortic curtain, raising suspicion of a perivalvular abscess. Blood cultures remained positive, and a new paravalvular leak developed during follow-up. Through serial multidisciplinary consultations, re-operation was judged to carry prohibitive risk, and the patient declined further surgery. Home-based palliative care with long-term suppressive oral linezolid was chosen in accordance with his preferences. He died peacefully at home with his family approximately 13 months after the index cardiac surgery and 10 months after recurrent bacteremia. Conclusions Recurrent S. caprae PVE with suspected perivalvular involvement in a BMT recipient poses difficult management decisions. Residual prosthetic or perivalvular infection is a plausible explanation, but re-infection cannot be excluded. When reoperation is high risk and inconsistent with the patient's wishes, ACP-guided palliative care with suppressive antimicrobial therapy may be an individualized option.

title: Two-dimensional speckle-tracking imaging for assessing cardiac dysfunction in liver cirrhosis: correlation with Child-Pugh score
authors: Jinhu Ma; Yan Ding; Haifeng Shao; Beiyu Zhang; Chunyu Jiang
abstract: BACKGROUND: Although two-dimensional speckle tracking imaging (2D-STI) enables sensitive and quantitative assessment of myocardial deformation, its application in patients with liver cirrhosis (LC) has largely been limited to ventricular function. This study applied 2D-STI to evaluate both ventricular and atrial function in order to identify early myocardial dysfunction in this population. METHODS: A total of 82 patients with LC were enrolled and stratified according to the Child-Pugh classification into Class A (n = 30), Class B (n = 29), and Class C (n = 23). Thirty healthy individuals served as controls. All 112 participants underwent conventional echocardiography and 2D-STI assessment. RESULTS: Compared with controls, all LC groups showed reduced left ventricular global longitudinal strain (LVGLS) and right ventricular free wall longitudinal strain (RVFWLS) (both P < 0.05), with a progressive decline from Class A to Class C. In contrast, right ventricular global longitudinal strain (RVGLS) was significantly decreased only in Classes B and C (P < 0.05). Left atrial conduit strain (LAScd) was significantly reduced across all LC groups (P < 0.05), whereas left atrial reservoir strain (LASr) and contractile strain (LASct) demonstrated a biphasic pattern -initially increased, then decreased- compared with controls. Overall, 2D-STI detected cardiac dysfunction earlier than conventional echocardiography. Significant negative correlations were observed between Child-Pugh score and LVGLS, RVFWLS, and RVGLS. CONCLUSION: Cardiac function is impaired in patients with LC and deteriorates with increasing disease severity. Compared with conventional echocardiography, 2D-STI detects cardiac dysfunction at an earlier stage, providing valuable support for early clinical intervention.

title: When Unilateral Pulmonary Edema Is Not Pneumonia: Fulminant Acute-on-Chronic Mitral Regurgitation Due to Spontaneous Chordal Rupture in Barlow’s Disease
authors: Nadia Loudiyi; Hafsa Erregui; Mohamed Malki; ZOUHAIR LAKHAL; Aatif Benyass
abstract: Unilateral pulmonary edema (UPE) is an uncommon and frequently overlooked manifestation of cardiogenic pulmonary edema that may mimic infectious pneumonia and is strongly associated with severe eccentric mitral regurgitation (MR), particularly in the setting of posterior leaflet prolapse or chordal rupture. We report the case of a 50-year-old woman with no previously known valvular heart disease who presented with abrupt-onset dyspnea at rest, rapidly progressing to severe respiratory distress and orthopnea within 24 hours. On admission, she was hypoxemic, with asymmetric crackles predominantly involving the right lung fields. Chest radiography demonstrated extensive right-sided alveolar infiltrates, initially raising suspicion of pneumonia. However, the absence of fever, systemic inflammatory response, and elevated infectious biomarkers prompted urgent cardiac evaluation. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed severe degenerative MR due to spontaneous chordal rupture, resulting in a flail P2 scallop extending into P3 on a background of Barlow’s disease, with a severe eccentric regurgitant jet. Despite initial stabilization with oxygen therapy, intravenous diuretics, and nitrates, the patient rapidly progressed to refractory cardiogenic shock requiring vasoactive and inotropic support. Urgent mitral valve surgery was indicated but could not be performed because of fulminant hemodynamic deterioration, and the patient died approximately two hours after admission to the cardiac intensive care unit. This case highlights a rare and catastrophic presentation of previously unrecognized degenerative MR in which spontaneous chordal rupture precipitated right-sided UPE and rapid hemodynamic collapse despite an apparently preserved left ventricular ejection fraction. It emphasizes that acute severe MR should be promptly considered in patients presenting with unilateral pulmonary infiltrates and acute respiratory failure when infectious features are absent. Early echocardiographic recognition and immediate surgical evaluation are crucial, as the therapeutic window before irreversible hemodynamic collapse may be extremely narrow.

title: Degenerative Mitral Regurgitation: From Prolapse to Precision Therapy
authors: Joanna Chikwe; Francesca Nesta Delling; Annetine C. Gelijns
abstract: Degenerative mitral valve regurgitation due to mitral valve prolapse affects ≈15 million people globally and is the commonest indication for mitral intervention in high-income countries, but its biology, natural history, and lifetime management are ill defined. This review summarizes current knowledge of the epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, risk stratification, and lifetime management of degenerative mitral regurgitation, with a focus on areas of uncertainty, recent advances, and emerging research directions. These include translational research focused on determining genetic and cellular drivers of disease progression and mechanistic studies geared to improve detection and prevention of downstream myocardial dysfunction, particularly in high-risk phenotypes, including arrhythmic mitral prolapse. The current landscape of randomized trials and large registries comparing contemporary surgical and transcatheter treatment and strategies to improve patient access to care and outcomes across all patient risk profiles and populations are also discussed.

title: Contents
Four-year clinical and echocardiographic outcomes of the Myval device in mitral, tricuspid, and pulmonary positions
authors: Akash Jain; Matteo Montorfano; Phillip Freeman; JOHN JOSE; Marcio Montenegro da Costa; Mussayev Abdurashid; Sengottuvelu Gunasekaran; Henrik Nissen; Pedro Martin; Ashok Seth; Krešimir Štambuk; Mario García-Gómez; Marcelo Rodríguez Murillo; Filippo Pensotti; Mathias Dyreborg Jørgensen; Mauricio Zúñiga; Cristhian Aristizabal; Carlos Cortés; Silvia Vallinas‐Hernández; Manuel Carrasco Moraleja; A. Jurado Román; Ignacio J. Amat-Santos
abstract: Introduction and objectives: Transcatheter implantation of balloon-expandable valves in non-aortic positions represents a growing off-label strategy for valve-in-valve and valve-in-ring procedures in high-risk patients. We assessed 4-year clinical outcomes and echocardiographic performance of the transcatheter heart valve Myval THV implanted in the mitral, tricuspid, and pulmonary positions. Methods: This retrospective multicenter study included a total of 50 patients (mitral n = 33; tricuspid n = 13; pulmonary n = 4) treated across 11 centers, with clinical follow-up extending to 4 years and echocardiographic assessment of surviving patients. Results: Technical successs was achieved in 96.9% of mitral cases (1 procedural death) and in 100% of tricuspid and pulmonary cases. At 1 year, death had occurred in 2/33 (6.1%) mitral patients and in none of the tricuspid or pulmonary patients. At 4 years, death had occurred in 4/33 (12.1%) mitral, 2/13 (15.3%) tricuspid, and 0/4 pulmonary patients; stroke occurred in 0/33, 1/13 (7.6%), and 0/4 patients, respectively. Mean transvalvular gradients at 4 years were 8.5 ± 3.3 mmHg (mitral), 3.8 ± 1.6 mmHg (tricuspid), and 12.7 ± 9.9 mmHg (pulmonary). No moderate or greater bioprosthetic regurgitation was observed at 4-year echocardiographic assessment, and no valve reinterventions were recorded during follow-up. Conclusions: In this multicenter cohort, off-label use of the Myval THV in non-aortic positions demonstrated adequate midterm clinical outcomes and sustained echocardiographic performance up to 4 years. These preliminary findings support the feasibility of this transcatheter approach in selected patients but require further prospective validation.

title: Quality control in degenerative mitral repair: repair rates, durability, benchmarking, and the reference center model
authors: Nadia H. Bakir; A. Marc Gillinov
abstract: Purpose of review The purpose of this report is to describe contemporary practice patterns and recommendations for the surgical management of degenerative mitral regurgitation. Recent findings The centralization of mitral valve surgery has allowed for expansion of minimally invasive approaches within a mentorship model, offering excellent patient outcomes. Approximately half of the national surgical volume is attributed to a relatively small group of experienced surgeons. Reoperation most commonly occurs due to technical failure, and re-repair at an experienced center offers better patient survival than replacement. There has been a sharp rise in transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) with limited understanding of late durability, although prior TEER decreases the likelihood of future surgical repair. Mild or less mitral regurgitation without stenosis defines the threshold for procedural success. In centers with both experienced surgeons and structural interventionalists, anticipated success of surgical repair is significantly higher, supporting the concept of a heart team model of multidisciplinary valve care. A modern quality improvement tool by the American Association of Thoracic Surgery, Adult Quality Gateway, has shown promise in both patient outcome reporting and risk assessment. Summary For patients with degenerative mitral regurgitation, early surgical referral to an experienced center with a multidisciplinary heart team is recommended.
